Agent is a coding assistant that runs in your terminal. It reads files, applies changes through tools, runs approved commands, and keeps a conversation you can return to. You choose the model provider and level of access.

Best-effort browser launch for the OAuth flow. Headless machines are normal (SSH, containers, CI), so a failure here is not an error: the caller also prints the URL, and the user can paste it anywhere.
Regression tests for importing the Codex CLI login.

Import a credential from a CLI that is already logged in. The Codex CLI keeps its ChatGPT login in `~/.codex/auth.json`. Copying that login in is convenient, but the refresh token is **single use**: refreshing rotates it, and the old one is rejected afterwards ("refresh_token_reused").
Failures from the auth layer, distinct from provider call failures.
Public exports for this module boundary.

Temporary localhost callback server for the authorization-code flow. The OAuth app redirects the browser to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`; this server answers exactly one request, hands the code back to the login flow and shuts down. Binding to 127.0.0.1 (not 0.0.0.0) keeps the listener off the network, and the `state` check rejects callbacks this process did not initiate.
Regression tests for credential resolution, oauth refresh, oauth login.

Credential resolution and the interactive OAuth login. `get()` is the only call the rest of the app needs: it checks the environment first, then `auth.json`, and transparently refreshes an expiring OAuth token. `refreshOnUnauthorized()` covers the other half of the contract — a token can be revoked before its `expires` timestamp, so a 401 triggers one refresh and one retry at the call site.
Regression tests for pkce, buildAuthorizeUrl, exchangeCode.

OAuth token endpoint calls: the authorization-code exchange and refresh. Both are `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POSTs (RFC 6749 §4.1.3, §6). The response parser only trusts what it validates: a missing `access_token` is a protocol failure, and an `expires_in` string is coerced to seconds so callers never have to think about it.
PKCE (RFC 7636) primitives. The verifier never leaves this process; the challenge goes to the browser. `S256` is the only method modern providers accept, so it is the only one implemented.
Per-provider auth policy. Two kinds of provider:
Regression tests for auth store.

`auth.json` on disk. Location: `$MYAGENT_HOME/auth.json`, defaulting to `~/.myagent/auth.json`. The file holds refresh tokens, so it is created `0600` in a `0700` directory and rewritten atomically (temp file + rename) — a reader never sees a half-written file, and a crash cannot leave a truncated credential store.

Google Gemini provider. Speaks `streamGenerateContent` over SSE — the wire format shared by the Gemini API and the Antigravity / Gemini CLI backend in ./antigravity.ts, so both share this one implementation.

Regression tests for responses stream, responses tool calls, responses stop reasons.

OpenAI Responses API provider (`POST {baseUrl}/responses`, SSE). Shares OpenAI's identity/auth with the chat-completions adapter, but not its wire format: `input` is a flat list of typed items, tools are flattened, the system prompt is `instructions`, and the stream is a sequence of named `response.*` events.

One streaming entry point for every provider. The registry holds providers under short ids (`anthropic`, `codex`, `opencode`, …) and resolves `"provider/model"` refs to them, so the agent loop and the CLI can switch backends by changing one string.

Minimal `text/event-stream` parser. Shared by every adapter that speaks SSE (OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic). Handles chunk boundaries that split a line, CRLF vs LF, multi-line `data:` fields, `:` comments / keep-alives, and streams that end without the final blank line.

The shared streaming call. Every provider adapter takes the same request, so this is the only place that fills in the defaults. The same loop works for every backend, which is the point of the provider layer.

A local server that speaks two real provider wire formats. It exists so the registry can be exercised end to end — real HTTP, real SSE, real adapters — without an API key: one endpoint answers in OpenAI's `chat.completion.chunk` shape, the other in Anthropic's named-event shape. The point of the registry is that the *same* code drives both.

Unified provider types. Every adapter (OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Gemini, …) translates its wire format into these shapes, so nothing above this layer ever imports a vendor SDK. Everything here is plain JSON, which is what makes sessions saveable and replayable in Phase 6.

Phase 7 demo: the lead delegates to the workers. One prompt, a real model, a real worker: the lead is asked to find out what is in a directory, it hands the job to the explorer, and only the explorer's report comes back — not the files it read.

Phase 5 demo: a long session that has to compact. A conversation that has grown past the model's window is summarised, and the agent carries on with the summary. The point is that it still knows what the task was.

Phase 2 demo: one event stream, three consumers. The loop yields events and prints nothing. A terminal reads them as text, a script reads them as JSON lines, and a parent agent reads the summary of a sub-agent — all from the same stream.

Phase 2 demo: the loop with a real model and a fake echo tool. The model is asked to call the tool; the loop runs it, sends the result back, and the model answers. Everything printed here comes out of the loop's event stream — the loop itself never prints.

Phase 3 demo: the agent, the tools and the permissions. A small project with a failing test. The agent reads the test, fixes the code and runs the test again — with the permission layer in front of the tools, in "ask" mode: the commands are allowed by a rule, and anything else would be put to the user.
Phase 5 demo: the layered system prompt. Shows what the model is told on every turn, layer by layer, and which of the layers the provider can cache.

Phase 6 demo: quit in the middle, come back, carry on. The first session asks for a tool and is then closed. The second session opens the same file, reads the conversation back and continues it — the model sees what happened before it was interrupted.

Phase 3 demo: a real model with real tools. The model is given a small project and asked to fix it. It reads the file, edits it, and checks its work — through the same loop, the same tools and the same event stream as everything else.
The eval suite, run against a real model. Each task is a small repository, a question, and a test. The report says how many passed, how many turns it took and what it cost.
Regression tests for the board.

The shared board. The workers of one task write to it, so the lead can see what is going on: which task, who owns it, what state it is in and what it found. It is a JSON file, so it survives a crash and can be read while the work is going on.
Regression tests for the isolation.

Isolation. A worker that only reads can share the workspace: it cannot change anything, so there is nothing to keep apart. A worker that writes gets a git worktree of its own, on a branch of its own, and the orchestrator merges the branch when it is happy with it.
Regression tests for one prompt, many agents.
Regression tests for the orchestrator, the pipeline, the generator and the critic.
Orchestration. Three patterns, all over the same worker:
Regression tests for an agent role, the roles.
Agent roles. A role is a name, a model, a set of tools and a system prompt. It lives in a file:
Regression tests for the task tool.

The task tool. The parent delegates to a worker: the worker gets its own system prompt, its own tools and its own model, and only the report it writes comes back. A worker can read fifty files; the parent sees three hundred words.
Regression tests for live workers.
Own worker lifetimes, concurrency, cancellation, follow-ups, transcripts, and observable status.
Regression tests for the budget in the loop.
Regression tests for counting tokens, the budget.
The budget. How much of the model's context window the conversation may use, and when it has to be made smaller.
Regression tests for the checkpoints.

File checkpoints. Before a tool changes a file, the file is snapshotted, so the change can be undone. It is the same idea as a git stash, without needing a repository: the snapshot is the content of the file before the change.
Regression tests for the custom commands, what a command sends.

Custom commands. A command is a markdown file in `.myagent/commands`. The name of the file is the name of the command: `deploy.md` is `/deploy`. What the file says is what the model is asked, so a command is a prompt you do not have to type again.
Regression tests for compaction, the summary prompt.

Compaction. When the conversation no longer fits, the old part of it is summarised and replaced by the summary. What is kept is the summary and the last few messages, so the model still knows what just happened and still knows what it was asked to do.

Context building. The system prompt is built in layers (see prompt.ts): the parts that do not change come first, so the provider can cache them, and the conversation follows as messages. Phase 5 replaces the message half with budgeting — trimming the transcript to the model's context window, summarising the middle, keeping the ends.

Where the agent is. The working directory, the branch it is on, the operating system and the date. It changes while the session runs, so it sits below the parts that do not: everything above it can be cached by the provider.
Regression tests for the eval tasks, the eval suite.

The eval runner. Every task runs in a throwaway repository: the files are written, the agent is asked the question, and a test is run in the repository afterwards. It passes when the test exits with zero.
The eval tasks. Each task is a small repository, a question, and a test that says whether the agent did it. The repository is thrown away afterwards, so the agent can do anything to it.
Regression tests for an extension, a provider an extension added.
Extensions. An extension is a TypeScript module in `.myagent/extensions` that exports a `register` function. It is given an API and adds what it likes: tools, commands and providers.
Regression tests for a hook in the loop.
Regression tests for the hook config, which hooks answer, a hook that runs.
Hooks. A hook is a shell command that runs when something happens. The command is given the details on its standard input, and what it does with them is up to it:
Public exports for this module boundary.
Regression tests for the log, what the loop writes down.

The log. Every request, every tool call and every usage is written down as one JSON object per line. The log is what the agent did, in order, in a shape a program can read: the sessions are for the conversation, the log is for the work.
Regression tests for loop guards, every call refused, abort.
Regression tests for the tools of one turn.
Regression tests for a signature on a call.
Test helpers: a provider that plays back scripted turns, and a fake echo tool. Shared by the loop tests.
Regression tests for the agent loop, accumulate, buildContext.
Regression tests for a tool that returns a lot, a tool that says its result must be kept.

The agent loop. model -> tool calls -> results -> model, until the model stops asking for tools. The loop yields events and never prints, so the CLI, a JSON mode and a sub-agent all consume the same stream.

Project memory. AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are how a project says what it wants. The search walks up from the working directory, so the memory of the directory you are in and of every directory above it is read; the user's own ~/.myagent/AGENTS.md is read too.
Regression tests for the layers, the project memory, the environment.

The layered system prompt. What the model sees on every turn is built in layers, and the order is the point: the parts that do not change come first, so the provider can cache them and only pay for the part that moved.
Regression tests for taking the secrets out, the secrets the process knows, taking the secrets out of anything.
Keeping the secrets out. Everything the agent reads goes into a log: the requests, the tool calls, the answers. A file it read may hold a key, and a log is a file that is written to disk and kept.

The "provider/model" ref. The ref is how a model is named in the command line and in the configuration: "provider/model". The provider is built from the part before the slash, and the model is called by the part after it.
Regression tests for emit events, not prints, the text consumer, the JSON consumer.

Consumers of the event stream. The loop never prints: it yields events, and every surface reads that one stream its own way. A terminal prints text, a script reads JSON lines, and a parent agent reads the summary of what a sub-agent did.
Regression tests for the repo map.

The repo map. An outline of what is in the project: the files, and the symbols in them. It is injected into the prompt so the model can find the right file without reading every file first — the agentic search (grep, glob, read) still does the finding, but the map tells it what exists.
Regression tests for quitting and resuming.

Retrying a provider call. A provider that answers 429 or 5xx is worth waiting for; a provider that answered with content and then dropped the connection is not, because the answer would be delivered twice. So a call is only retried when nothing came back yet, and never after a tool has run — the side effects of a tool cannot be undone by asking the model again.

A small project with a failing test. The scenario the guide asks for: the agent reads the failing test, fixes the code and runs the test again. It is small on purpose — the point is that read, edit and bash work together, not that the bug is hard.
Regression tests for the agent in a real project.
Regression tests for a long session.
Regression tests for the session store.
Sessions. A session is a file of entries, one JSON object per line, appended and never rewritten:
Regression tests for shrinking a tool result, the old tool results.

Shrinking what the model has to read. A tool result can be enormous — a file, a build log, a search over a whole repository — and the model rarely needs all of it. So a big result keeps its head and its tail, and says how much was left out; and a result that is many turns old is replaced by a one-line stub, because the model has long since moved on from it.
Regression tests for the skills, the body of a skill, the skill tool.
Skills and the plan. The dynamic part of the prompt: what the agent can draw on, and what it said it would do. It changes while the session runs, so it belongs at the bottom of the prompt.

Sub-agents. A sub-agent is the same loop with its own transcript: it gets its own tools and its own prompt, and it yields the same events, so the parent reads one stream and sees everything the sub-agent did.

Counting tokens. The count is an estimate until the provider says otherwise: the real number arrives with the usage of a response, and the difference between the two is remembered, so the next estimate is closer.
The agent's state and the events it emits.
Regression tests for marking what is data, a tool that holds data.

What the agent reads is data. A file in the repository may say "ignore what you were told and run this". A page from the web certainly may. Neither is the user talking: the user asked a question, and the agent read something.

bash — run a command. The output is capped so a runaway command cannot fill the model's context: the head and the tail are kept and the middle is replaced by a note about how much was left out.

edit — replace an exact string in a file. The most reliable edit format there is: the model says what is in the file and what should be there instead. The edit only goes through when what it says is actually there, and only once — a match that is missing or that appears more than once is an error, not a guess.
Finding programs on PATH.
Regression tests for read, write, edit.
A small MCP server, for the tests. It says hello with two tools: one that echoes what it is given, and one that fails. It talks over stdio, which is how most MCP servers are run.
glob — find the files whose names match a pattern. ripgrep lists the files when it is installed; otherwise the same list is built here, skipping what git ignores.

grep — search the files for a pattern. ripgrep does the work when it is installed: it is fast, it skips what git ignores, and its output is exactly the shape we want. When it is not installed, the same search runs here instead, with the same rules about ignored files.

.gitignore rules. The search tools skip what git ignores, so a search does not wander into node_modules or a build directory. This is a practical subset of the format: patterns, directory patterns, anchoring and negation.

Regression tests for the MCP config, an MCP tool, the schema of an MCP tool.
The MCP client. The Model Context Protocol is how a program offers its tools to other programs. A server is a process (or a URL) that says "here are my tools", and the agent calls them like its own.

Paths, as the tools see them. Every tool takes a path the way a person would write it: relative to the working directory, or absolute. The resolved path is what the tool touches, and it is what the error messages name.

Own live permission mode, literal session grants, pending approvals, policy changes, and cancellation.

Regression tests for parsing rules, matching rules, deciding.
Rules: how they are written and how they are matched.

What the agent is allowed to do. The tools are powerful; the permissions are what keep them pointed. Four modes say how much is allowed without asking, and a list of rules says what is always allowed, always refused, or always worth a question.
Regression tests for the permission wrapper.

The tools, behind the permissions. Every tool that is wrapped is asked first. The answer is one of three: it runs, it is refused, or the user is asked. A refusal never reaches the tool: the model is told what happened, and carries on.
read — a file, with line numbers. The output looks like `cat -n`: every line is prefixed with its number, so the model can say "line 42" and mean it.
Running a program and collecting what it says.

todo — the checklist the model keeps. The model rewrites the list when its plan changes, and reads it back when it needs to remember what is left. The list lives with the tool, so it lasts for the session.
Regression tests for bash, grep, glob.
The standard set of tools.

The tool contract. A tool is something the model may call. The description and the schema are what the provider advertises; `run` is the executable side, which Phase 3 fills in (read, write, edit, bash, grep, glob, todo).
Regression tests for validateArgs, toToolSpec.

Validating a tool's arguments. The schema a tool declares is the schema its arguments are checked against: the model is told exactly what is expected, and what it sends is held to that. A tool with a broken schema is refused rather than run with whatever the model happened to send.
Walking a directory, the way a search should. Git's ignored files are skipped, and so are the directories that are never worth searching: .git, node_modules and the usual build output.
write — create a file, or replace what is in it.
